Recent research supports testing order and recency separately. “Does It Look Sequential?” (2024) compares original and shuffled histories across 15 datasets, finding weak sequential structure in several popular benchmarks. RecSys 2025 work distinguishes user behavior patterns from item-availability effects using constrained shuffling; consequently, shuffle sensitivity alone cannot establish reliance on evolving intent. [2024 study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.12008), [2025 study](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748042).

BERT4Rec diagnostics must match its masked prediction interface: hide the target, append the reserved MASK for next-item inference, and score from that position. The original paper explicitly motivates masking to prevent target leakage through bidirectional attention. Proposed engineering controls: identity transformations should preserve scores; deliberately corrupted MASK IDs or readout positions should trigger diagnostic failures. These controls are recommendations, not a standardized benchmark identified in this search. [BERT4Rec](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.06690v2).

Recommended stress suite: use training-prefix/next-item pairs with identical candidates across perturbations; compare recent deletion against equally sized older/random deletion; shuffle earlier history while preserving the latest item. Report paired changes in HR@10, target rank and score margin, with bootstrap intervals resampling users together with all their prefixes. Keep the pinned evaluator unchanged: sampled metrics can reverse model comparisons and do not establish full-catalog performance. Interpret perturbation differences as model sensitivity, with deletion also changing length and positional context—not as causal evidence of intent. [Sampled-metric analysis](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/).
